extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and graduate students studying or evaluating inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT) and related arithmetic-geometry researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for communicating, disseminating, and judging mathematical understanding of inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT): what counts as adequate exposition, who counts as an expert, how to evaluate students/referees, and anti-patterns to avoid. Focuses on practices for producing accessible records, pedagogy, and community interactions specific to IUT but with generalizable points for mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed, explicit, mathematically substantive, and readily accessible written exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a detailed, explicit, mathematically substantive, and readily accessible written exposition as an alternative to direct mathematical discussions (email, video, face-to-face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such written exposition is 'of fundamental importance' and 'would be of great value not only for professional mathematicians and graduate students... but also for scholars in the [perhaps distant] future.' It should be sufficiently explicit to permit independent verification and historically avoids confusions (examples: Fermat's Last Theorem, debates of Galileo/Einstein). The author repeatedly emphasizes this exact phrasing as the desired form of communication and as the starting point for long-term infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain long-term infrastructural apparatus for confronting, disseminating, and developing mathematics (LTInfr)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and maintain long-term infrastructural mechanisms whose starting point is production of detailed, accessible written expositions to confront, disseminate, and further develop mathematical disputes and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a historical point of view the only meaningful technical tool to overcome deadlocks is producing such written expositions; this infrastructure is required to avoid recurring socio-political confusions (cf. (LTInfr)). The document links this requirement to examples and sections referenced (BlkAcc, (UndIg), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of autonomy of understanding (definition of an 'expert')
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert is judged by 'the extent to which the level of understanding ... enables the mathematician to "stand on his/her own two feet" with regard to various assertions concerning the theory, on the basis of independent, logical reasoning, without needing to be "propped up" or corrected by [the author] or other known experts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not strictly well-defined, this criterion is operationalized by observed abilities: (Atm1) detect minor errors/oversights in IUTchI-III; (Atm2) propose new insightful viewpoints; (Atm3) propose modifications to strengthen/streamline the theory; (Atm4) produce technically accurate oral or written expositions; (Atm5) supervise/train others who then demonstrate Atm1–Atm4. Different experts may demonstrate different subsets of these abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required attributes and time commitment for those who will gain solid understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: To attain a solid, technically accurate understanding of IUT typically requires 0.5–2 years of substantial time and effort, and participants should be sufficiently familiar with numerous classical theories in arithmetic geometry, be motivated/enthusiastic, mathematically talented, and have sufficient time to devote to study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes typical study periods (roughly half a year to two or three years depending on factors) and that successful learners include professional mathematicians and graduate students; gives an existence example of a graduate student achieving understanding largely by self-study with limited contact. This is presented as a practical criterion for evaluating readiness and likely success of dissemination/training efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase number of professionals with solid technical understanding and willingness to discuss
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to increase the number of professional mathematicians (e.g., in arithmetic geometry) who have a solid technical understanding of the mathematical content of contentious assertions (e.g., the RCS) and who are prepared to discuss them with the IUT community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper regards both producing detailed expositions and increasing such knowledgeable interlocutors as in the interest of both the IUT community and critics (RCS). The author reports roughly ~10 mathematicians have achieved sufficient understanding to make independent, confirmed statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting heuristically based beliefs for rigorous proof (Voodoo Hypothesis / Blf=Pf)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristically supported beliefs cannot serve as substitutes for rigorous mathematical proofs; invoking heuristic 'surely' arguments (the 'Voodoo Hypothesis') to cast doubt on a proof is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that such heuristics often lead to mischaracterization of rigorous mathematicians as 'mindlessly obedient zombies' and play a central role in disputes about IUT (cf. Examples and RCS-IUT). This entry also ties into (MthAcc): truly impartial positions require mathematically accurate understanding, not ignorance or heuristic doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware and reject fabricated reformulations not logically related to original theory (avoid RCS-IUT style simplifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformulations or simplifications of a mathematical theory are problematic when they are substantively different from and have no direct logical relationship to the original theory; fabrication of such versions (e.g., RCS-IUT) spawns misleading social/political drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents that fabricated versions are often motivated by wishful simplification and are amplified by distorted media/internet coverage; such versions produce lurid dramas unrelated to substantive mathematics and therefore should be identified and rejected. Reformulations are acceptable only if based on thorough, accurate understanding and demonstrable direct logical relationship to the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate discussions on substantive mathematical content rather than social/political/psychological aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing IUT (or similar theories), focus on substantive mathematical content and avoid getting sidetracked by non-mathematical interpretations (social, political, psychological) which distract and amplify confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concentration is asserted as 'of the utmost importance' to avoid vicious spirals of media distortion and fabricated versions; the author uses this as justification for terminology choices (use of 'RCS') and for focusing efforts on exposition and expert discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop pedagogical materials and evaluation exercises (Ev1–Ev3) to assess understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Create suitable exercises/examination problems, evaluation schemes for junior mathematicians, and refereeing/evaluation criteria for papers to educate and evaluate students and mathematicians learning IUT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that developing analogues of Ev1 (exercises), Ev2 (evaluating junior mathematicians), and Ev3 (refereeing) for IUT is still under development; many technical issues can be reformulated as exercises or exam problems to assess autonomy of understanding. These are recommended tools for dissemination and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer verification requires shared conceptual framework to be socially meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Although certain arguments can be formalized and verified by computer, such computer verification becomes socially/politically meaningless if parties do not share or recognize the abstract conceptual mathematical framework underlying the formalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses the simple proof of irrationality of sqrt(2) as an example: formalization is technically easy, but without shared acceptance of the formal framework the verification does not resolve disputes. This warns against relying on technical formal verification alone as a remedy for sociopolitical disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose modes of mathematical interaction (physical travel vs electronic) by cost–benefit '≫' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer electronic interactions (email, online video) where travel's required effort, time, and cost '≫' the expected mathematical or non-mathematical gain; do not coerce travel when costs far exceed benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses geographical vs mathematical proximity and notes travel can be taxing financially and mentally, with cultural differences adding friction; travel decisions should respect the inequality of effort vs gain. Physical meetings are still valuable when they are meaningfully so, but coercion is ineffective long term.
